summary: Specifies a framework for building HIP-based overlay networks. HIP handles connection management, while other functions such as data storage and retrieval are done by other peer protocols. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a plan for building a network of cooperating computers on top of the internet, using HIP to manage who connects to whom.

questions: how does hip bone handle connections
what is the hip base exchange
subtitle: A framework for building overlay networks using the Host Identity Protocol.

tldr.problem: Overlay networks need to manage connections between nodes, handle NAT traversal, and support mobility while different peer protocols handle data storage and network maintenance independently.
tldr.mechanism: HIP BONE uses HIP (Host Identity Protocol) as a unified layer for connection management and security across overlay networks, allowing any peer protocol to build on top of it for domain-specific tasks.
tldr.outcome: Overlay networks can reuse HIP's connection management, NAT traversal, and mobility features instead of each peer protocol implementing them separately, reducing complexity and promoting consistency.

facts.label: Security mechanism
facts.value: IPsec ESP and public key authentication

today: RFC 6079 is an experimental specification defining a framework for HIP-based overlay networks. The framework itself remains experimental, though HIP and its extensions have been explored in various projects. The framework provides guidance for building specific overlay instances, such as the RELOAD protocol instantiation.

sections.title: What HIP BONE Solves
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) defines a new layer between the network and transport layers that separates host identifiers from IP addresses. This identifier/locator split makes HIP ideal for building overlay networks—networks constructed on top of the existing IP network.

Instead of each overlay network protocol reinventing connection management, NAT traversal, and mobility features, HIP BONE provides a framework where HIP handles these common tasks. Other functions like data storage, retrieval, and overlay maintenance are handled by peer protocols specific to each overlay's needs.
sections.plainLanguage: HIP gives computers a stable identity that doesn't change when they move to a different location. This is helpful for overlay networks where computers might be in different places.

sections.title: How HIP Works
sections.content:
Identifiers and locators: HIP uses 128-bit ORCHIDs (Overlay Routable Cryptographic Hash Identifiers) as stable identifiers. Computers identify each other by these identifiers, not by IP addresses, which are treated only as locators—temporary addresses where a host can be reached.

The HIP base exchange: Two hosts establish a connection through a four-message handshake: the initiator sends I1, receives R1 from the responder, sends I2, and receives R2. The responder includes a cryptographic puzzle in R1 to protect against denial-of-service attacks.

Locator changes: If a host moves to a new IP address, its identifier stays the same, so ongoing connections survive the change. The update exchange allows hosts to exchange new locator information.

Security: HIP provides encryption and integrity protection of data traffic using IPsec ESP. Hosts authenticate each other using public keys, either through certificates or the leap-of-faith mechanism similar to SSH.
sections.plainLanguage: HIP gives each computer a fingerprint (identifier) based on its secret key. Computers use this fingerprint to find and trust each other, not their IP addresses. This way, if a computer moves to a new address, friends can still recognize it.

sections.title: The HIP BONE Framework
sections.content:
HIP BONE combines HIP with peer protocols in a layered architecture. The peer protocol handles overlay topology, maintenance (nodes joining and leaving), and data storage and retrieval. HIP handles connection establishment and lightweight message exchanges between nodes.

The HIP-with-peer-protocol stack: Architecturally, HIP sits as a thin waist layer above IPv4 and IPv6. The peer protocol creates a signaling layer on top of HIP to set up forwarding paths for HIP messages, similar to how OSPF provides routing information for IP.

Routing tables and forwarding: The peer protocol maintains routing tables using Node IDs (typically HIP identifiers). When HIP needs to forward a packet, it converts the routing table into a forwarding table to select the next hop. This allows HIP to route packets through the overlay according to the overlay's topology.
sections.plainLanguage: HIP BONE is like a two-level postal system. HIP handles envelopes—making sure messages reach the right computer and stay safe. The peer protocol handles the delivery route—figuring out which path the message should take through the overlay network.

sections.title: Connection and Message Exchange
sections.content:
Establishing connections: In HIP BONE, when a node wants to connect to another node through the overlay, it sends an I1 packet that is forwarded hop-by-hop through the overlay toward the destination. The overlay acts as a rendezvous service, allowing connection establishment even if the nodes do not know each other's IP addresses. If intermediate nodes have active connections protected with IPsec ESP, the I1 packet travels over these protected channels. Otherwise, nodes forward it directly if they know the next hop's IP address.

NAT traversal: HIP's NAT traversal is based on ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment), where nodes gather address candidates and perform STUN-based connectivity checks. The HIP base exchange performs an ICE offer/answer exchange, allowing nodes to discover which address pairs work for communication.

Lightweight queries: For simple query-response exchanges that do not require a full connection, HIP BONE allows forwarding single HIP messages through the overlay. The integrity of the payload is protected, and the overlay provides the rendezvous service.
sections.plainLanguage: To connect, one computer sends a message into the overlay network, and intermediate computers pass it along until it reaches the destination. If computers are already connected, they send it through their secure tunnel. The system also checks which path works through NAT.

sections.title: Overlay-Specific HIP Parameters
sections.content:
HIP BONE defines two new HIP parameters for overlay use.

OVERLAY_ID parameter: All HIP messages sent via an overlay MUST contain an OVERLAY_ID parameter to identify which overlay the message belongs to. This is necessary because a host may participate in multiple different overlays simultaneously. The instance specification for each overlay type defines how the identifier is generated to prevent collisions.

OVERLAY_TTL parameter: This optional parameter carries a Time-to-Live value that decrements at each overlay hop. If a host receives a packet with TTL of zero and is not the final recipient, it MUST drop the packet and send back a notification error indicating the TTL was exceeded. The TTL mechanism prevents messages from looping indefinitely through the overlay.
sections.plainLanguage: When computers send messages through an overlay, they add two labels: one saying which overlay network to use, and one saying how many hops the message can take before giving up.
